unit.title: Prepare and present appetizers and salads

essays.stem: Explain why salads and cold appetisers are high-risk foods, and describe how you would keep them safe while you prepare them.
essays.modelAnswer: Salads and cold appetisers are ready-to-eat foods. They are not cooked again before the guest eats them, so any bacteria that get onto them will not be killed. Many contain high-risk items such as cooked chicken, seafood, eggs, rice and mayonnaise. To keep them safe, I wash my hands well before I start and after touching raw food, bins or my face. I wear a clean uniform and hair cover. I wash all fruit and vegetables in cold water. I use clean boards and knives kept for salad and fruit (green in the usual code), never boards used for raw meat or fish. I handle the food with clean tongs or clean disposable gloves, not bare hands. I keep the ingredients in the fridge at 5 °C or below until I need them, and I prepare small batches so food is not left out for long. Finished items are covered, labelled with the name and date, and put back in the fridge above any raw meat until service.
markingPoints: Explains ready-to-eat: no further cooking to kill bacteria; high-risk ingredients
Hand washing, clean uniform and hair cover
Wash produce; separate clean boards and knives for salad
Use tongs or gloves, not bare hands
Keep chilled at 5 °C or below; small batches; cover, label and store above raw food

essays.stem: Describe how to make and present a tray of canapés for a reception.
essays.modelAnswer: I plan the number I need, usually a few per guest, and choose canapés with different colours, flavours and textures. I prepare the parts in advance: the bases, such as small toasts, crackers, pastry cases or bammy rounds; the spreads, such as butter or cream cheese; the toppings, such as Solomon Gundy, smoked marlin or shrimp; and the garnish, such as herbs or thin slices of pepper. I keep the toppings covered in the fridge. Close to service, I spread each base thinly right to the edges, so the topping does not make it soggy. I add the topping neatly, the same amount on each, so every canapé is the same size and only one or two bites. I add a small edible garnish. I use clean gloves or tongs. I arrange them on a clean, chilled platter in neat rows or in odd-number groups, not too crowded, with each kind together. I keep the tray covered and chilled until it goes out, and I label it with any allergens.
markingPoints: Plans the number and a mix of colours, flavours and textures
Prepares bases, spreads, toppings and garnish in advance; keeps toppings chilled
Spreads to the edge to stop sogginess; assembles close to service
Same size and amount on each; one or two bites; edible garnish; gloves or tongs
Neat display on a chilled platter, covered and chilled, allergens labelled

essays.stem: Describe how to prepare and present a tossed green salad with a vinaigrette dressing.
essays.modelAnswer: I choose fresh, crisp leaves, such as lettuce, and other salad items such as cucumber, tomato, sweet pepper and onion. I wash my hands, then wash the leaves in cold water, take off any damaged leaves, and dry them in a salad spinner or on clean cloths, because wet leaves water down the dressing. I tear the leaves into bite-size pieces and slice the other items neatly on a clean salad board. I keep them in a covered bowl in the fridge until near service. To make the vinaigrette, I whisk about 3 parts oil with 1 part vinegar or lime juice, a little mustard, salt and pepper, and taste it with a clean spoon. Just before serving, I toss the leaves lightly with a little dressing so they are coated but not soaked, because dressing makes the leaves go limp if it is added too early. I pile the salad on a chilled plate or bowl to give height, add the colourful items on top, wipe the rim and serve at once.
markingPoints: Wash leaves in cold water, remove damaged ones, dry well
Tear or cut items neatly on a clean salad board; keep chilled
Vinaigrette about 3 parts oil to 1 part acid, seasoned and tasted with a clean spoon
Dress lightly, just before serving (reason given)
Present with height and colour on a chilled plate with a clean rim

essays.stem: Describe how to make mayonnaise by hand, how to save it if it splits, and the food safety steps you would take.
essays.modelAnswer: I use pasteurised egg yolks, because the mayonnaise is not cooked and raw eggs can carry Salmonella. All the ingredients should be at the same cool room temperature. I put the yolks in a clean bowl, set on a damp cloth so it does not move, and whisk in a little mustard, salt and a spoon of vinegar or lime juice. I add the oil drop by drop at first, whisking all the time, until the sauce starts to thicken. Then I add the rest of the oil in a thin stream, still whisking, until it is thick and glossy. I taste it with a clean spoon and add more acid or seasoning. If it splits, because the oil went in too fast or it was too cold, I put a fresh yolk or a spoon of warm water in a clean bowl and slowly whisk the split sauce into it. I put the mayonnaise in a clean, covered container, label it with the date, and keep it in the fridge at 5 °C or below, using it within the time the Centre's food safety plan gives.
markingPoints: Pasteurised yolks (reason: raw egg risk); ingredients at the same temperature
Yolk with mustard, seasoning and acid; bowl steadied
Oil added drop by drop, then in a thin stream, whisking all the time
Fix a split sauce by whisking it slowly into a fresh yolk or a little warm water
Covered, labelled, chilled at 5 °C or below, used within the allowed time

essays.stem: Describe how to make Jamaican potato salad with beetroot safely, from cooking the potatoes to storing the salad.
essays.modelAnswer: I wash and peel Irish potatoes and cut them into even dice, about 2 cm, so they cook at the same time. I boil them in salted water until just tender, so they hold their shape. I also boil the beetroot until tender, then peel and dice it, wearing gloves because it stains. I boil eggs for about 10 minutes, cool them in cold water and peel and chop them. I cool all the cooked items quickly, spread on shallow trays, and chill them in the fridge before mixing, because warm potatoes in mayonnaise let bacteria grow. I dice onion and sometimes carrot and sweet pepper. When everything is cold, I mix the potato, beetroot, egg and onion gently with mayonnaise, a little mustard, salt and pepper, so the beetroot turns the salad pink. I taste with a clean spoon. I put it in a covered container, label it with the name, date and allergens (egg and mustard), and keep it in the fridge at 5 °C or below until it is served, and I do not leave it out longer than the Centre's food safety plan allows.
markingPoints: Even dice; potatoes boiled until just tender
Beetroot and eggs cooked and prepared; gloves for beetroot
Cooked items cooled quickly and chilled before mixing (reason given)
Mixed gently with mayonnaise and seasoning; tasted with a clean spoon
Covered, labelled with date and allergens, chilled at 5 °C or below; time out limited

essays.stem: Explain the main rules for presenting appetisers and salads so that they look attractive.
essays.modelAnswer: Good presentation makes guests want to eat the food. I choose the right plate or platter: clean, with no chips, chilled for cold food and a size that suits the portion. I use colour, by mixing green leaves with red tomato, orange carrot, yellow pepper or pink shrimp, so the plate is bright. I give the food height, by piling salad in the middle rather than spreading it flat. I keep the portion right, as the standard recipe says, so every plate looks the same and the cost is right. I place items neatly and leave some space, so the plate is not crowded. On platters, I set canapés in straight rows or in odd-number groups, with each kind together. I use a small garnish that can be eaten and suits the dish, such as a herb sprig or a lime wedge, not something large or bitter. I add the dressing or sauce neatly, and I wipe the rim with a clean cloth. Finally, I serve the food quickly so it is still fresh and at the right temperature.
markingPoints: Clean, suitable, chilled plates or platters
Colour contrast and height
Correct, even portions as the standard recipe says; not crowded
Neat arrangement (rows or odd numbers); small edible garnish that suits the dish
Clean rim and quick service at the right temperature

essays.stem: Explain how you would set up and look after a cold appetiser and salad display on a buffet.
essays.modelAnswer: Before service, I check that the buffet table and equipment are clean, and that chilled display units or trays of crushed ice are ready to keep the food at 5 °C or below. I set out the food close to service time, in small or medium dishes rather than one huge bowl, and keep the rest in the fridge to top up. Each dish has its own clean serving spoon or tongs, and a sneeze guard is used if the Centre has one. I put a label by each dish with its name and the main allergens, such as nuts, egg, fish or shellfish. During service I check the temperature of the food with a clean probe and write it down. I keep the display tidy, wipe up spills and replace used utensils. When a dish runs low, I bring a fresh dish rather than tipping new food on top of old. I watch the time each dish has been out, and anything left longer than the Centre's food safety plan allows is thrown away. At the end, leftover food that has been on display is thrown away.
markingPoints: Clean set-up with chilled units or ice to keep food at 5 °C or below
Small dishes put out close to service, the rest kept in the fridge
Separate serving utensils; labels with names and allergens
Temperature checks recorded; tidy display; replace dishes, never top up old food
Time limits kept; food left out too long, or left at the end, thrown away

essays.stem: A guest at a function is allergic to nuts and eggs. Explain how you would choose and prepare a safe appetiser and salad for them.
essays.modelAnswer: First, I make sure the allergy is written on the order and that the chef knows. I choose dishes with no nuts and no eggs, for example a tossed green salad with a plain oil and lime dressing, and plantain chips or crudités with a dip made without egg or nuts. I check every recipe and every label, including dressings, sauces, bread and crackers, because many contain egg or traces of nuts, and mayonnaise is made with egg. If I am not sure about any item, I leave it out and ask the chef. Before I start, I wash my hands and clean and sanitise the work area. I use clean boards, knives, bowls and utensils that have not touched nuts or eggs, and I make the guest's dish first or apart from the other dishes. I cover the plate, mark it clearly as the allergy order, and hand it to the server, telling them which guest it is for, so it reaches the right person. If the kitchen cannot make it safely, the guest is told honestly.
markingPoints: Allergy recorded and the chef told
Choose dishes with no nuts or eggs (suitable example given)
Check all recipes and labels, including dressings and bases; ask if unsure
Clean equipment and area; make it apart to avoid cross-contact
Plate covered and marked; handed over for the right guest; honest if it cannot be made safely

essays.stem: Describe how you would make stamp and go (saltfish fritters) as a hot appetiser for a reception.
essays.modelAnswer: The day before, or a few hours ahead, I soak the saltfish in cold water, changing the water, or boil it in two changes of water, to take out most of the salt. I drain it, remove all the skin and bones, and flake it finely. I make a batter with flour, baking powder, a little salt and black pepper, and enough water to make a thick, smooth batter. I stir in the flaked saltfish with finely chopped onion, scallion, thyme, tomato and a little Scotch bonnet pepper, cut wearing gloves. I heat oil in a heavy pan or fryer to about 170–180 °C, following the fryer maker's instructions. I drop spoonfuls of batter into the oil, away from me, and do not overcrowd the pan. I fry them until they are golden and crisp on both sides and cooked through, then drain them on kitchen paper. I keep them hot at about 63 °C or above and serve them soon, so they stay crisp, on a platter with a dip such as a pepper sauce. I tell guests they contain fish and wheat.
markingPoints: Soak or boil the saltfish to remove salt; remove skin and bones; flake
Make a thick batter and add the fish and seasonings (gloves for the pepper)
Fry in hot oil at a suitable temperature, laid in away from the body, in small batches
Fry until golden and cooked through; drain
Hot-hold at about 63 °C or above, serve soon; allergens (fish, wheat) made known

essays.stem: Compare simple and compound salads, and name the four parts of a plated salad, giving an example of each part.
essays.modelAnswer: A simple salad is made with one main item, or one main kind of item, and a dressing. Examples are a tomato salad with vinaigrette, a cucumber salad, or a green salad of lettuce leaves. A compound salad, also called a mixed salad, is made from several different items mixed or arranged together, often with a richer dressing. Examples are Jamaican potato salad with beetroot and egg, coleslaw, a Caesar salad, or a chicken salad. Compound salads can be served as a main course, while simple salads are often a side dish. A plated salad has four parts. The base is usually a bed of clean lettuce leaves, which lines the plate. The body is the main part, such as diced chicken or shrimp. The garnish adds colour and finish, such as tomato wedges, chopped herbs or a slice of lime. The dressing adds flavour and moisture and holds the salad together, such as vinaigrette or mayonnaise.
markingPoints: Simple salad: one main item with a dressing, with an example
Compound salad: several items, with an example
Base: e.g. bed of lettuce
Body: the main item, e.g. chicken or shrimp
Garnish and dressing, each with an example

practical1.title: Canapé and hot appetiser platters for a reception of 20 guests
practical1.brief: As a group, prepare and present canapés and a hot appetiser for a reception of 20 guests, about 3 cold canapés and 2 hot pieces per guest. Make three kinds of cold canapé, for example Solomon Gundy on crackers, callaloo and cream cheese on bammy rounds, and smoked marlin or shrimp on cucumber slices, and one hot item: stamp and go (saltfish fritters). Each member takes charge of one kind of canapé or the fritters: they prepare the parts, then make at least 15 pieces of the same size, with the assessor watching. All members help to set out two chilled platters and one hot platter, and write the allergen labels. Keep the cold platters covered in the fridge, and the fritters hot, until the assessor checks them. Photograph each stage below and add the photos to the group's practical. Hand in once for the whole group when the platters are done and the area is clean.
materials: Crackers, bammy, cucumbers, bread for toast bases
Smoked herring (or ready-made Solomon Gundy), cream cheese, butter, callaloo, smoked marlin or cooked shrimp
Saltfish (soaked the day before), flour, baking powder, onion, scallion, thyme, Scotch bonnet pepper
Herbs, sweet peppers and limes for garnish
Cook's and paring knives, boards in the Centre's colour code, piping bag or spoons
Frying pan or fryer, oil, slotted spoon, kitchen paper
Platters, cling film, allergen labels, probe thermometer, disposable gloves
photos: The mise en place: bases, spreads, toppings and garnish laid out
Each member's canapés being put together, with gloves or tongs
The fritters frying, and draining on kitchen paper
A close-up showing canapés of the same size and neat garnish
The two cold platters and the hot platter, finished, with allergen labels
The probe reading for the cold platter and for the fritters
The work area cleaned and sanitised
checklist: Washed hands, wore a clean uniform and hair cover, and used gloves or tongs for ready-to-eat food
Prepared the bases, spreads, toppings and garnish in advance and kept toppings chilled
Spread bases to the edges and made canapés of the same size, one or two bites each
Fried the fritters safely until golden and cooked through
Arranged a neat platter with colour, even spacing and an edible garnish
Kept cold food at 5 °C or below and hot food at about 63 °C or above
Cleaned and sanitised the work area and equipment
safety: Use clean tongs or clean disposable gloves for ready-to-eat food
Wear gloves for Scotch bonnet pepper and do not touch your eyes
Lay fritters into the oil away from you; never leave hot oil unattended
Keep knives on the board, point away, and wash them straight after use
Wipe up spills at once and put out a wet-floor sign

practical2.title: Salad bar: four salads, two dressings and a chilled display
practical2.brief: As a group, prepare a salad bar for 20 guests with Jamaican potato salad with beetroot, coleslaw, a tossed green salad, and a tropical fruit salad, and two dressings: a vinaigrette and a mayonnaise made by hand with pasteurised egg yolks (or as the assessor says). Each member takes charge of one salad and helps with the dressings: they wash and prepare the ingredients, cook and cool anything that needs cooking, and mix and season the salad. The group sets up a chilled display, on ice or in a chilled unit, with a serving utensil and a name and allergen label for each dish. Dress the green salad only when the assessor is ready to check it. Each member takes and records the temperature of their salad with a clean probe. Photograph each stage below and add the photos to the group's practical. Hand in once for the whole group when the display is done and the area is clean.
materials: Irish potatoes, beetroot, eggs, onion for potato salad
Lettuce, cucumber, tomatoes, sweet peppers for the green salad
Local fruit: pineapple, mango, pawpaw, watermelon, limes
Oil, vinegar, lime juice, mustard, pasteurised egg yolks, salt, pepper
Salad spinner, graters, knives, boards in the Centre's colour code, mixing bowls, whisk
Display bowls, crushed ice or chilled unit, serving utensils, labels, cling film
Probe thermometer, temperature log sheet, detergent, food-safe sanitiser, cloths
photos: All produce washed and the mise en place laid out
The cooked potato, beetroot and egg cooling on shallow trays
The vinaigrette and the finished mayonnaise
Each salad mixed, in its display bowl
The salad bar set up on ice or in the chilled unit, with labels and utensils
The probe reading for each salad, and the completed temperature log
The work area cleaned and sanitised
checklist: Washed hands and all produce, and used the right boards and clean knives
Cooked and cooled the potato salad items quickly before mixing
Made a vinaigrette in about the right proportion and a stable mayonnaise
Prepared their salad neatly, with even cuts, and tasted it with a clean spoon
Dressed the green salad just before it was checked
Kept every salad at 5 °C or below and recorded the temperature
Labelled each dish with its name and allergens, with its own serving utensil
Cleaned and sanitised the work area and equipment
safety: Use the guard when grating or using a mandoline, and keep fingers clear
Use pasteurised yolks for the mayonnaise, as the Centre's food safety plan says
Wear gloves when handling beetroot and ready-to-eat food
Carry knives point down and never try to catch a falling knife
Wipe up water and ice spills from the floor straight away
